## February 29, 1960 — A Monday That Comes Once Every Four Years

You were born on a day that doesn't exist most years. That is not a poetic flourish; it is a calendrical fact. February 29 appears only in years divisible by four, with exceptions so arcane they were last relevant in 1900. In 66 years of life, the date of your birth has appeared on a calendar exactly 16 times after that first Monday morning. You are, in the precise sense, 16 years old and 66 years old simultaneously.

---

**Twenty years before you arrived, on this exact date, history was made in Hollywood.** On February 29, 1940, Hattie McDaniel became the first Black American to win an Academy Award, taking Best Supporting Actress for *Gone with the Wind* at a ceremony she had to enter through a side door. She sat at a segregated table, separated from her white co-stars. Her victory was genuine; the conditions around it were a precise diagram of American contradiction. You were born on the 20th anniversary of that moment, into a country that was, in the same weeks, being asked again to decide what it actually believed about equality.

**On the day you were born, the ground shook in Morocco.** The Agadir earthquake struck on February 29, 1960, a shallow, violent rupture directly beneath one of Morocco's fastest-growing coastal cities. In a matter of seconds, roughly a third of Agadir's population was killed — perhaps 12,000 people. The city was effectively destroyed and had to be rebuilt from the ground up. It was one of the deadliest earthquakes of the twentieth century, and it happened on the same rare Monday that you arrived.

**Twenty-eight days before your birth, four Black college students sat down at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave.** The Greensboro sit-in of February 1, 1960 ignited a movement: within weeks, sit-ins were spreading to dozens of cities across the South. By the time you were drawing your first breaths, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee was forming, and the Civil Rights Act — still four years away — was becoming imaginable. You were born at the precise acceleration point of the civil rights movement.

**1960 was called the Year of Africa.** Seventeen African nations gained independence in the twelve months surrounding your birth — Cameroon, Senegal, Mali, Madagascar, Congo, Somalia, Benin, Niger, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Chad, the Central African Republic, Gabon, Nigeria, Mauritania, and others. The post-war dissolution of European empires, which had been building for a decade, reached a flood in the year you were born. The map of the world was being redrawn in real time.

**The space race was barely three years old.** Sputnik had shocked the West in 1957. NASA had existed for less than two years when you were born. Alan Shepard would not become the first American in space until May 1961 — you were fifteen months old. You were born at the absolute beginning of the human attempt to leave the planet, and you lived to see rovers on Mars, a private space industry, and a telescope that images galaxies thirteen billion light-years away.

---

**The arithmetic of a leap day life.**

Most people born in 1960 have celebrated their birthday 66 times on the calendar. You have celebrated it 16 times on the actual date. February 29 fell in 1964 (you turned 4, or 1), 1968, 1972, all the way through 2024. In non-leap years — which is to say, three years out of every four — your birthday simply does not exist. You have spent most of your life in that condition: technically ageless by the calendar, obliged to choose a neighboring date, knowing that your real day is quietly absent.

**The arc of 66 years.**

You were born into a world of rotary phones and three TV channels, where space travel was science fiction that had just barely become fact. You grew up through the Kennedy assassination, Vietnam, Watergate. You were 29 when the Berlin Wall came down. You watched the internet go from curiosity to infrastructure in less than a decade. You saw smartphones make the entire accumulated knowledge of civilization available in a shirt pocket.

And you've done all of it on a schedule that most people don't share — a birthday that appears and disappears on a four-year cycle, a small reminder that the calendar is a human invention, approximate and negotiated, and that you arrived on one of the days where its seams show most clearly.

Sixteen real birthdays. A world unrecognizable from the one you entered. Both things are true.
